## Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- The abstract of the technical report (reports/technical-report.pdf), copied as it stands; keep the two in step.
Its one citation is written out with its DOI, since the page has no bibliography. -->

Autonomous scientific discovery requires more than generating plausible hypotheses: scientific claims must remain
traceable to evidence, open to criticism, and experimentally falsifiable. Starting from the C9orf72-associated
T-cell autoreactivity reported by Michaelis et al. ([Nature, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09588-6)),
we investigate a central question: **Can a multi-agent system autonomously transform a biomedical observation
into auditable, mechanistically explicit, and falsifiable therapeutic hypotheses for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
(ALS)?**

We implement a twelve-phase workflow combining literature retrieval, independent hypothesis generation, adversarial
review, evidence verification, computational analysis, experimental design, and therapeutic synthesis. The system
builds on _Claude Code_'s dynamic workflows for multi-agent coordination, while a deterministic Python orchestrator
controls phase execution, validation, and persistent state. An append-only knowledge base represents scientific
claims, provenance, supporting and contradicting relationships, and epistemic status.

We evaluate five end-to-end runs under identical configurations, comparing three executions with an initially
empty knowledge base against two using accumulated knowledge. All runs generated structured research proposals;
two returned a proposal outcome and three reported insufficient evidence. Deterministic biomedical analyses were
reproducible, but agent-generated interpretations and evidential relationships remained vulnerable to
overstatement. Notably, accumulated knowledge enabled the construction of longer mechanistic chains (12 and 13
edges) without increasing the number of edges verified against their own source (one per chain), although a few
agent-proposed edges were supported indirectly by other verified evidence.

These findings demonstrate the feasibility of integrating scientific agents into an auditable discovery workflow
while exposing a limitation of persistent agentic knowledge: structural coherence and knowledge accumulation do
not necessarily imply stronger evidential support. The system generates falsifiable therapeutic hypotheses but
establishes neither validated causal mechanisms nor therapeutic efficacy.
